## Summary

Many-analyst studies are an emerging format of crowdsourced scientific analysis [@Schweinsberg2021], in which multiple analysts independently answer the same research question using the same dataset [@Voracek2019; @Silberzahn2018]. Several high-profile studies demonstrate that results and conclusions can be highly contingent on subjective but defensible analytical decisions [@Silberzahn2018; @Botvinik-Nezer202; @Breznau2021; @Huntington-Klein2021; @Hoogeveen2022; @Coretta2023], arising from disagreement about modelling strategy or variation in data preparation [@Voracek2019; @Simonsohn2020]. Similarly to meta-analysis, many-analyst studies treat analytical variation as the object of study, and produce rich metadata for each analysis — including model type, transformations, and variable selection — that can be used to characterise analytical uncertainty. Unlike meta-analysis, the source of variation under study is analytical rather than arising from sampling or measurement error between independent datasets.

`ManyEcoEvo` is an R package that provides a structured, reproducible workflow for conducting the statistical analyses characteristic of many-analyst studies. The package implements a pipeline that: standardises heterogeneous analyst estimates onto a common scale; fits multilevel meta-analytic models across multiple analyst submissions; computes each analyst's deviation from the meta-analytic mean; and fits a series of univariate regression models examining how analytical choices relate to deviation from the consensus estimate among teams. The pipeline is built around a nested tibble structure that allows the full sequence of operations to be mapped systematically over multiple datasets and over systematically varied analytical subsets of those datasets — for example, subsets defined by peer-review quality ratings, variable collinearity, or analyst expertise. This architecture makes repeated application of the analysis pipeline across many dataset variants a tractable problem.

Although `ManyEcoEvo` was developed for the 'Same Data, Different Analysts' study in ecology and evolutionary biology [@Gould2025], its workflow generalises to computationally analogous problems. Collaborative big-team open science projects (e.g. '[ManyBirds](http://themanybirds.com/)' [@ManyBirdsProject2025], '[ManyBabies](https://manybabies.org/)' [@ManyBabies; @McMillan2026], '[ManyPrimates](https://manyprimates.github.io/)' [@ManyPrimates]) and coordinated distributed experiments (e.g. '[NutNet](https://nutnet.org/)' [@Borer2014], '[DragNet](https://dragnetglobal.org/)' [@Borer2025]) produce multiple datasets that pose similar data-manipulation and analysis challenges. The package also generalises to sensitivity analyses in conventional meta-analyses, where the primary analysis is repeated across varied inclusion criteria or data subsets.

In addition to the workflow infrastructure, `ManyEcoEvo` ships the curated, analysis-ready datasets from @Gould2025 as package data objects. These include analyst effect-size estimates and metadata, out-of-sample predictions as an alternative outcome variable, peer-review ratings, and variable-use data for two research questions — one from evolutionary biology (blue tit nestling growth) and one from conservation ecology (*Eucalyptus* seedling recruitment). The packaged data enables straightforward reproduction and re-analysis of the published results.

## Statement of Need

Conducting a many-analyst study requires solving a class of data-management and analytical problems that existing meta-analytic software does not address. The primary challenge is heterogeneity: analyst submissions span a wide variety of modelling approaches, response variable transformations, and link functions, all of which must be identified, back-transformed, and standardised onto a common scale before any synthesis is possible. In a study involving over a hundred analyst teams, performing this step manually — tracing each analyst's reported transformation, applying the appropriate back-transformation, and propagating the result through to a standardised effect size or out-of-sample prediction — is extremely time-consuming and error-prone.

A second challenge is systematic repetition. Many-analyst studies - especially like @Gould2025 where different analysis questions were posed - require the full many-analyst pipeline to be repeated across multiple analytical subsets. For example, on subsets; with analyses that were rated as low quality by peer reviewers, or that contained highly collinear predictors; with extreme outliers removed; that were restricted to expert analysts. Without dedicated infrastructure, this repetition is implemented as bespoke, study-specific scripts: copies of the primary analysis, manually adapted for each subset. This approach makes it difficult to reason about what differs between subsets and what does not, obscures whether observed differences in results across subsets are attributable to the subset definition or to incidental differences in the code, and makes it hard to verify that the same analytical protocol has been applied consistently. It also makes the analysis difficult to reproduce, audit, or adapt to new data.

The target audience for `ManyEcoEvo` is therefore researchers conducting or re-analysing many-analyst studies, as well as researchers whose work involves the systematic repetition of a meta-analytic pipeline across multiple datasets or analytically defined data subsets. This includes teams running collaborative big-team open science projects where data are collected across multiple experiments, locations or analyst groups. A secondary audience is conventional meta-analysts for whom sensitivity analyses, which repeat the primary meta-analysis under varied inclusion criteria, are a routine but currently ad hoc component of their workflow.

`ManyEcoEvo` addresses these challenges by providing a reusable, programmatic workflow that treats outcome-variable harmonisation and standardisation, subset generation, and pipeline repetition as first-class operations. Standardisation and back-transformation of heterogeneous analyst estimates are handled by a family of functions that identify and apply the appropriate transformation for each analysis, making the process explicit, auditable, and reproducible. Subset generation is implemented as row-expansion of a nested tibble, so that the full downstream pipeline — meta-analysis, computation and transformation of deviation scores, and univariate regressions — propagates automatically through all dataset and subset combinations without modification to the pipeline itself. This architecture makes it straightforward to verify that the same analytical protocol has been applied consistently across all subsets, and to isolate the effect of each subset definition on results. Together, these properties support FAIR [@Wilkinson2016] and reproducible research practice in a study format that is otherwise difficult to implement in a principled way.

## State of the Field

The R ecosystem for meta-analysis is mature and well-characterised. Lortie & Filazzola [-@lortie2020] provide a structured contrast of the two most widely used packages in ecology and evolutionary biology: meta [@meta], a direct and intuitive choice for rapid implementation of general meta-analytic statistics, and `metafor` [@metafor], a more comprehensive package suited to complex multilevel models. Both provide heterogeneity estimation, visualisation tools, and publication bias diagnostics, and both are widely used across ecology, evolution, and the social sciences. For visualisation, `orchaRd` [@orchaRd] extends `metafor` with orchard plots suited to ecological effect-size data, and `metaviz` [@metaviz] provides additional forest and funnel plot variants. These packages form the analytical foundation on which `ManyEcoEvo` builds: the multilevel meta-regression at the core of the package is implemented via `metafor::rma.mv()`, and forest plots are produced using conventions established by `orchaRd` and `metaviz`. However, all of these packages share a common design assumption — that the unit of analysis is a single meta-analytic dataset, and that the researcher's task is to fit, interrogate, and visualise one model. None provide infrastructure for the upstream data-wrangling challenges specific to many-analyst data, nor for the systematic generation and propagation of analytical subsets through a complete pipeline. Contributing the `ManyEcoEvo` workflow to any of these packages would require introducing a fundamentally different data model and pipeline architecture that sits outside their intended scope.

A second category of potentially relevant tools comes from multiverse analysis and specification curve analysis. The `multiverse` package [@Sarma2023] provides an embedded domain-specific language for declaring alternative analysis paths within R and R Notebooks, implementing the multiverse analysis philosophy of @Steegen2016. `specr` [@Masur2020] provides utilities for conducting and visualising specification curve analyses [@Simonsohn2020], allowing users to set up, run, evaluate, and plot the full space of analytical specifications for a single dataset. `Boba` [@Liu2021] extends this further with an integrated domain-specific language and interactive visualisation system for authoring and interpreting multiverse analyses across multiple programming languages. These tools share with `ManyEcoEvo` the goal of characterising how analytical variation affects results, but they operate in a fundamentally different setting: they generate variation in analysis outcomes programmatically from a single analyst's declared decision space, rather than synthesising analytic variation across many analysts or teams. Consequently, they do not address the resolution of incompatibility between analyst estimates arising from different model specifications, transformations, and link functions prior to meta-analytic synthesis, nor the nested data structures that arise when analyst submissions must be aggregated and compared. The conceptual framing is also distinct: multiverse and specification curve tools ask "what would have happened if this analyst had made different choices?", whereas `ManyEcoEvo` asks "given that many analysts made different choices, what can we infer about the distribution and drivers of those differences?" Contributing the `ManyEcoEvo` pipeline to any of these tools would require introducing a meta-analytic synthesis layer and a model for resolving heterogeneous-input data that are outside their design scope entirely.

The closest precedents for the `ManyEcoEvo` approach are the study-specific analysis repositories published alongside individual many-analyst studies, such as those accompanying the 'ManyBabies' [@ManyBabies] and 'ManyPrimates' [@ManyPrimates] projects. These repositories demonstrate that the analytical problems `ManyEcoEvo` addresses recur across disciplines. However, their code is written for a single study and dataset, with no abstraction or reuse intended. Contributing to these repositories would produce more study-specific code rather than a reusable, generalisable tool. `ManyEcoEvo` was therefore developed as a standalone package because no existing tool addresses the combination of resolution of heterogeneity in outcome variables, nested data management, systematic subset generation, and reproducible pipeline repetition that many-analyst studies require.
